strengths: The motivating example clearly demonstrates why both contextual information and intervention-scope selection matter. Controlling X1=-C achieves expected reward 1/3, exceeding the best constant intervention and the policy controlling both variables.
Combining existing possibly optimal mixed policy scopes with contextual Bayesian optimisation provides a useful framework for continuous intervention problems.

The experiments use a common HEBO implementation, 110 random seeds, and uncertainty bands. They examine cases where baselines can and cannot attain the optimum, alongside noise and redundant-variable experiments.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.1 is not established by the supplied proof. Appendix A applies single-GP confidence bounds to the randomly selected optimal function without simultaneous control over the m functions; taking maximum smoothness constants does not resolve this selection issue. The time-uniform union bound also requires summability of 1/pi_t, whereas the manuscript specifies summability of pi_t. These gaps affect a central theoretical contribution.

The theorem analyzes Algorithm 1, not the proposed MAB-UCB-plus-HEBO Algorithm 2. Each outer arm's reward distribution changes as its contextual optimiser learns. The observation that rewards become stationary at optimality does not justify stationary-UCB confidence bounds during learning. No analysis controls this learning-induced bias, and declining normalized regret over 700 iterations does not establish asymptotic sublinear regret.

The theoretical novelty is limited. Algorithm 1 can be expressed as ordinary GP-UCB on the disjoint union of the function domains, using a block-diagonal kernel. Its regret is standard optimisation regret on that domain. Together with the reliance on existing POMPS theory and HEBO, this makes the contribution primarily an integration of established components unless stronger results are provided.

Definition 3.3 conflicts with the reported POMPS examples because it requires strict superiority over every other mixed scope. In Appendix D, a scope controlling X2 using C1 and C0 can reproduce every policy using only C1 by ignoring C0. Consequently, the latter cannot strictly dominate all alternatives. The definition needs an explicit treatment of redundant scopes or equivalence classes.

The evaluation does not isolate the proposed scope-selection mechanism. The CaBO comparisons have only one CoCa-BO candidate scope, so their improvements cannot demonstrate an advantage of outer UCB selection. Comparisons against uniform allocation and alternative selectors over identical POMPS sets are missing. All environments are constructed SCMs, which limits evidence of practical significance.

Scalability claims exceed the evidence. The large-variable example mainly adds redundant variables and still has only two POMPSes. There is no systematic evaluation as the number of candidate scopes grows, nor timing or memory measurements for scope enumeration. Parallelising an exponential search does not establish general computational scalability.

Experimental specifications contain consequential inconsistencies. Appendix B.2 omits Cancer from the PSA equation although its subsequent completion-of-squares derivation requires that term. Appendix E states Var(Y)=1/3+Var(epsilon_Y), but Appendix C.1 implies 0.01/3+0.01 Var(epsilon_Y) under the optimal policy. These discrepancies undermine verification of the reference optimum and claimed noise severity.

Reproducibility is incomplete: although a framework release is claimed, the supplied manuscript gives no repository location or software version. Outer-UCB exploration settings and complete intervention domains are also unspecified.
